title: Beyond the scale: Bringing a whole-health approach to GLP-1 weight management
summary: Weight management is changing quickly, and for many primary care practices, GLP-1–based therapies are becoming part of everyday patient conversations.
body_markdown:
Weight management is changing quickly, and for many primary care practices, GLP-1–based therapies are becoming part of everyday patient conversations.


For patients using GLP-1–based therapies, the scale can show whether weight is changing. But it cannot show the full picture of metabolic health, nutritional status, or other factors that may be relevant throughout treatment. Research also shows that significant weight loss can include lean mass loss, while gastrointestinal effects are common with GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy.1,2,3


For practices beginning to incorporate a more whole-person approach, laboratory testing can help add a broader perspective without requiring an entirely new model of care.


## Start with the questions you're already asking


Adopting a more whole-person approach does not have to mean ordering extensive testing for every patient. It can begin with a familiar clinical question: **What else should I understand about this patient's health as their weight changes?**


Baseline testing can help establish a starting point.


Labcorp's[Weight Management Baseline Profile](https://www.labcorp.com/tests/318798/weight-management-baseline-profile) combines a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), HbA1c, and lipids. Additional options include a profile[with TSH](https://www.labcorp.com/tests/321052/weight-management-baseline-profile-with-tsh) and another[with a liver evaluation](https://www.labcorp.com/tests/258998/weight-management-baseline-profile-with-liver-evaluation) incorporating FIB-4. With GLP-1 receptor agonists now demonstrating benefits in reducing MASH, liver health may be an increasingly important consideration when establishing a metabolic baseline.


A[Weight Management Follow-Up Test](https://www.labcorp.com/tests/311959/weight-management-follow-up-profile) includes HbA1c and lipids to help assess changes in glycemic status and lipid parameters that may occur alongside weight loss and lifestyle modification.


For physicians already managing patients with complex, interconnected chronic conditions like[cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/understanding-cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic-syndrome) ,[dyslipidemia](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/2026-accaha-dyslipidemia-guideline-update) , and[liver disease](https://www.labcorp.com/biopharma/central-labs/therapeutic-experience/mash) , these measures can fit naturally into existing workflows while helping connect weight management with patients' broader health pictures.


The goal is not necessarily **more testing** . It is **more purposeful testing** .


## Watch what's changing beyond weight


Weight loss is only one measure of clinical progress.


For patients using GLP-1–based therapies, changes on the scale may be the most visible measure of progress, but they do not provide a complete view of the patient’s health. Looking at relevant metabolic and nutritional measures can help providers understand what else may warrant attention as treatment progresses.


Nutrition may be an important consideration, particularly for patients experiencing persistent gastrointestinal symptoms, reduced dietary intake, or other risk factors for nutritional inadequacy. Gastrointestinal effects, including nausea, diarrhea, constipation, and vomiting, are commonly reported with GLP-1 receptor agonists, and the effects of these therapies on gastrointestinal physiology and gastric emptying are well documented.¹˒³


That does not mean every patient receiving GLP-1–based treatment needs comprehensive nutritional testing. Instead, the patient’s history, diet, symptoms, treatment experience, and existing health risks can help determine when additional investigation may be appropriate.


## Go deeper when the patient gives you a reason


Routine[weight management testing](https://www.labcorp.com/treatment-areas/weight-loss-management) may be enough for some patients. Others may present with a more complex cardiometabolic history, nutritional concerns, or other factors that warrant additional evaluation.


[Labcorp Whole Health Solutions](https://www.labcorp.com/providers/whole-health-solutions) provides curated testing options across areas including cardiometabolic risk, nutritional status, and hormone and endocrine health. That allows providers to start with familiar testing and expand selectively based on what they see in the individual patient.


**If cardiometabolic risk is a concern** , the Advanced Cardiometabolic Biomarker Panel* evaluates 21 biomarkers, including ApoB, GlycA, hs-CRP, Lp(a), Lp-PLA2, and an NMR Lipoprofile with lipids and LP-IR.


For a provider accustomed to standard lipid and glucose testing, this can offer an avenue for deeper investigation when routine measures do not provide the level of information needed for an individual patient's risk assessment.


**If nutritional status raises questions** , the Comprehensive Nutrient Panel* evaluates 11 biomarkers, including ferritin, folate, iodine, magnesium, zinc, and vitamins A, B12, C, D, and E, along with CRP.


Again, the value is in selecting testing based on the patient's clinical profile, rather than automatically adding a broad panel because a patient is using a weight loss medication.


**If the patient has more complex health concerns** , the Longevity and Vitality Panel* evaluates 71 biomarkers across cardiometabolic risk, endocrine conditions, inflammation, nutritional deficiencies, and kidney and liver function. Components include HbA1c, insulin, a lipid panel, ferritin, folate, vitamin B12, vitamin D, free T3, free T4, and TSH, among others.


This creates a flexible progression: **start with the immediate clinical need, then investigate more deeply when appropriate.**


## Make a whole-health approach workable in everyday practice


For an independent practice, adding functional or integrative principles does not have to mean building a separate program or dramatically changing how care is delivered. Weight management offers a practical entry point because many of the clinical questions already overlap with preventive care and chronic disease management.


A practical approach might look like:


- **Establishing a baseline** using testing appropriate to the patient’s weight management plan and health history
- **Identifying where deeper investigation may be useful** , whether around cardiometabolic health, nutritional status, or another concern
- **Selecting additional testing with a clear purpose** , rather than applying the same comprehensive panel to every patient
- **Using follow-up testing to track relevant changes** and inform next steps


This builds on something independent primary care already does well: connecting information across visits and conditions rather than treating weight management as an isolated service.


Labcorp Whole Health Solutions can help make expansion more approachable. Seven curated panels* provide defined starting points, while a tailored test menu of more than 1,000 biomarkers built from the company's broader menu of more than 6,500 tests allows providers to explore specific questions as they arise. More than 700 specialized MDs and PhDs are also available for consultation on application in care.


## A practical step toward more personalized care


GLP-1–based therapies have expanded the options available for weight management,4 but weight is rarely the only consideration in a primary care visit. CKM risk, liver disease, nutritional concerns, and other chronic conditions may all be part of the same clinical picture. Testing can help connect overlapping concerns, uncover factors that may influence treatment, and provide objective measures to guide care over time.


For primary care practices exploring whole-person care, the opportunity is about making each test count, **turning useful clinical insights into better-informed care while supporting a healthier, more sustainable practice.**
